entries.title: FULL NODE
entries.body: A computer that runs a client of the Bitcoin protocol, and which downloads, verifies and stores the entire blockchain, i.e. the complete transaction history since the Genesis block. A full node independently verifies all transactions and blocks according to Bitcoin's consensus rules. It is therefore this type of node that provides the highest level of verification for its user, and that makes it possible to reduce to the maximum the need to trust a third party. The full node requires more storage resources, computing power, RAM and bandwidth than a lightweight node (SPV).

entries.title: LIGHTNING NODE
entries.body: A computer that runs an implementation of the Lightning Network (Eclair, LND, Core Lightning...). A Lightning node is set up on top of a Bitcoin node, and makes it possible to create and manage bidirectional payment channels between different users. Lightning nodes are connected to one another, which forms a network of payment channels. These channels make it possible to carry out an almost unlimited number of transactions without needing to publish them individually on the Bitcoin blockchain.

entries.title: NAKAMOTO SATOSHI
entries.body: Pseudonym of the person or group who created Bitcoin and wrote its original white paper in 2008 (White Paper). Nakamoto, who communicated only online, eventually disappeared from the public scene in 2011.

entries.title: NAMECOIN
entries.body: The first altcoin in Bitcoin's history, launched in April 2011. Namecoin is a fork of the Bitcoin source code that aims to provide a decentralized system for registering and managing domain names, as an alternative to the traditional DNS (*Domain Name System*). Its main use case is the `.bit` extension, which allows censorship-resistant domain names to be registered directly on the blockchain.

entries.title: NAT - NETWORK-ADJUSTED TIME
entries.body:
An estimate of universal time based on the clocks of the network's nodes. Each node calculates its NAT by taking the median of the time differences between its local clock (UTC) and those of the nodes it is connected to, then adding its local clock to the median of these differences, up to a maximum of 70 minutes. The *network-adjusted time* is therefore a median of the nodes' time, calculated locally by each node. This reference is then used to verify the validity of block timestamps. Indeed, for a block to be accepted by a node, its timestamp must lie between the MTP (median time of the last 11 mined blocks) and the NAT plus 2 hours:

```text
MTP < Horodatage valide < (NAT + 2h)
```

entries.title: NBITS
entries.body:
A 4-byte field present in the header of every Bitcoin block, which encodes the difficulty target in a compact form: the first byte indicates the number of bytes of the full target (the exponent), and the following three bytes make up the mantissa (the significant digits of the target). The decoding formula is: `cible = mantisse \times 256^{(exposant - 3)}`.

A block hash must be less than or equal to the target value encoded in `nBits` for the block to be considered valid. This field is recalculated every 2,016 blocks during the difficulty adjustment, in order to maintain an average interval of about 10 minutes between blocks.

entries.title: NERDMINER
entries.body: An *open source* solo Bitcoin mining project that runs on ESP32 microcontrollers. Created by BitMaker in 2022, it lets you assemble a small, very low-power miner to discover concretely how mining works. The device can be connected to a solo mining pool such as Public Pool. With a *hashrate* of about 78 kH/s, the chances of finding a block are astronomically low, but the project is above all educational and playful. NerdMiner displays real-time statistics about hashing and the Bitcoin network on its built-in screen.

entries.title: NESTED SEGWIT
entries.body: A script standard used to wrap native SegWit scripts within a P2SH script. Nested SegWit scripts were invented at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. They make it possible to use this new standard even with services or *wallets* that are not yet natively compatible with SegWit. It is a sort of transitional script toward the new standard. Today, it is therefore no longer very relevant to use this type of *wrapped* SegWit script, since most *wallets* have implemented native SegWit.

entries.title: NEUTRINO
entries.body:
A lightweight Bitcoin client written in Go and developed by Lightning Labs. Designed for mobile applications using the Lightning Network, Neutrino implements the *compact block filters* protocol defined in BIP-0157 and BIP-0158 to synchronize the blockchain while minimizing bandwidth and storage.

Neutrino downloads only block headers and compact filter headers. Filters and full blocks are loaded on demand when a match is detected with the watched scripts. It offers *rescan* features to scan the blockchain for relevant transactions, as well as a `GetUtxo` function to verify the existence and spent status of an output.

Neutrino is notably used as a *backend* by LND for lightweight setups that do not require a full Bitcoin Core node. The term "Neutrino" is sometimes used loosely to refer to the BIP-0157/0158 protocol itself, whereas it designates only this specific client library.

entries.title: NFT
entries.body:
Acronym for *Non-Fungible Token*. An NFT represents a unit of bitcoin that, by users of a protocol external to Bitcoin, is interpreted as non-fungible and associated with the ownership of an asset external to Bitcoin, such as an image or any other type of data.

On Bitcoin, protocols such as Ordinals and Stamps allow the creation and management of these NFTs. These protocols are often controversial, because their activity clutters the blockchain with non-financial data. This can have negative consequences for the system, notably by inducing an increased operational load for full nodes or by raising transaction fees through the influence of external economic factors.

entries.title: NIP
entries.body: A technical specification that defines a feature, format or expected behavior in the Nostr protocol. NIPs play a role analogous to Bitcoin's BIPs: they are community documents that formally describe how clients and relays must implement a given feature. Each NIP has a number and covers a specific aspect of the protocol. With the exception of NIP-01, which describes the base protocol that everyone should implement, NIPs are optional and backward-compatible. A NIP can be marked as `unrecommended` when it is deprecated or replaced by a more recent specification. The official NIPs repository is maintained on GitHub and open to contributions.

entries.title: NLOCKTIME
entries.body:
A 4-byte field built into every Bitcoin transaction, which specifies either an absolute block height (if its value is below 500,000,000) or an absolute Unix timestamp (if its value is greater than or equal to 500,000,000). The transaction is considered final (and therefore includable in a block) only once this value is strictly exceeded by the height of the candidate block (for height mode) or by the MTP, the median of the 11 previous blocks (for time mode). It is therefore an absolute timelock, as opposed to the relative timelocks of the `nSequence` field, and it acts at the level of the entire transaction.

The `nLockTime` is enforced only if at least one input of the transaction has a `nSequence` different from the value `0xFFFFFFFF`. If all inputs have `nSequence = 0xFFFFFFFF`, the field is completely ignored. This is why wallets using the `nLockTime` typically set `nSequence = 0xFFFFFFFE`.

`OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` complements this mechanism by making it possible to impose a timelock from a `scriptPubKey`. The opcode checks 4 conditions:
* the value at the top of the stack and the transaction's `nLockTime` are of the same type (block height or timestamp),
* the value at the top of the stack is not negative,
* the value at the top of the stack is less than or equal to the transaction's `nLockTime`,
* the `nSequence` of the input being evaluated is not `0xFFFFFFFF`.

CLTV therefore never directly checks the time or the height: it delegates this verification by forcing the spending transaction to declare a `nLockTime` less than or equal to the value wanted by the script.

entries.title: NO2X
entries.body: Name of the campaign launched in August 2017 following the lock-in of the SegWit soft fork, whose goal is to convince users not to implement the doubling of the block size from 1 MB to 2 MB as planned in the SEGWIT2X update.

entries.title: NODE
entries.body:
In the Bitcoin network, a node is a computer that runs a client of the Bitcoin protocol (such as Bitcoin Core, for example). It participates in the network by maintaining a copy of the blockchain, by relaying and verifying transactions and new blocks and, optionally, by taking part in the mining process. The sum of all Bitcoin nodes represents the Bitcoin network itself.

There are several types of nodes on Bitcoin, including full nodes and lightweight nodes. Full nodes keep a complete copy of the blockchain, verify all transactions and blocks according to the consensus rules, and actively participate in the broadcasting of transactions and blocks on the network. By contrast, lightweight nodes, or SPV nodes (*Simple Payment Verification*), keep only the block headers and rely on full nodes to obtain information about transactions. 

*Some people also distinguish so-called "pruned" nodes ("*pruned node*" in English). These are full nodes, which download and verify all blocks since the Genesis block, but which keep only the most recent blocks in memory.*

entries.title: NODL
entries.body: A company founded in late 2018 that designs turnkey Bitcoin and Lightning Network nodes, in the form of ready-to-use hardware boxes. Nodl was the first manufacturer to integrate BTCPay Server, to enforce Tor by default on all its devices, and to offer full disk encryption with a physical security switch (*kill switch*). The company also offers nodl Cloud, an infrastructure service hosted in its own data centers (Paris, Geneva, Zurich) for individuals and businesses who want to run nodes without managing the hardware.

entries.title: NOISE
entries.body: A cryptographic framework used to establish and authenticate connections between Lightning nodes. The Noise protocol, specified in BOLT-08, defines the initial *handshake* during which two nodes exchange their keys and negotiate an encrypted session. It relies on a Diffie-Hellman key exchange with ephemeral and static keys, in order to have properties of persistent confidentiality (*forward secrecy*). Once the *handshake* is complete, all communications between the two nodes are encrypted and authenticated. Noise replaces the TLS or SSH protocols usually used in network applications, with a simpler specification better suited to the constraints of the Lightning Network.

entries.title: NONCE
entries.body:
In the context of computing, the term "nonce" designates a number used only once, then replaced. It is often random or pseudo-random. It is used in various cryptographic protocols to guarantee the security of the process. For example, the ECDSA signatures used within the Bitcoin protocol involve the use of a nonce. This means that this number must be new for each signature. If it is not, it is possible to calculate the private key used by comparing two signatures that use the same nonce.

Nonces are also used in the mining process on Bitcoin. Miners increment these modifiable values within their candidate blocks. They change the value of the nonce in order to find a cryptographic fingerprint less than or equal to the difficulty target. This process requires a great deal of computing power, because it is an exhaustive search among a large number of possible nonces. When a miner finds a nonce which, when included in its block, produces a hash meeting the difficulty criteria, the block is broadcast to the network, and the miner wins the reward.

*In 2010, researchers discovered that Sony's PlayStation 3 used the same nonce when signing different packets of code. This reuse of the nonce allowed attackers to calculate the private key used to sign the software. With the private key in hand, the attackers could create valid signatures for any code, which allowed them to run unauthorized software, including pirated games or custom operating systems, directly on the PS3.*

*There is a common misconception about the origin of the term "nonce". Some claim that it stands for the abbreviation of "number only used once". In reality, the origin of the word goes back to the 12th century and comes from the semantic evolution of the Middle English expression "for then anes", which meant "for this occasion".*

entries.title: NOSTR
entries.body: An open and decentralized communication protocol, whose acronym stands for *Notes and Other Stuff Transmitted by Relays*. Created by fiatjaf in 2020, Nostr relies on a simple architecture: clients cryptographically sign events (the protocol's unique data structure) and publish them to relays, servers that store and redistribute these events. A user's identity is a pair of cryptographic keys on the secp256k1 curve, the same one used by Bitcoin. No central server controls access or content: if a relay censors a user, that user can migrate to other relays without losing their identity or their audience. Nostr is closely linked to the Bitcoin ecosystem, notably through the native integration of *zaps* (Lightning micropayments) and the use of the same cryptographic infrastructure. The protocol is extensible thanks to NIPs (*Nostr Implementation Possibilities*), community specifications that define event formats and features. Beyond *micro-blogging*, Nostr serves as a foundation for a variety of applications: encrypted messaging, long-form articles, *marketplaces*, closed groups or even code collaboration via Git.

entries.title: NPUB
entries.body: The encoding format of the Nostr public key in Bech32, defined by NIP-19. The `npub` prefix identifies a Nostr public key. The raw public key is a 32-byte number on the secp256k1 curve, derived from its private key. The npub encoding adds a human-readable prefix (`npub1...`), a checksum to detect input errors, and uses an alphabet excluding ambiguous characters. The npub is the public identifier of a Nostr user: it can be shared freely and allows anyone to find the associated profile and posts. Unlike the nsec, it does not compromise the security of the account if it is disclosed.

entries.title: NSEC
entries.body: Bech32 encoding (NIP-19) of a Nostr secret (private) key, with the prefix `nsec`. The key corresponds to a 32-byte value used as a secret on secp256k1; it makes it possible to produce the Schnorr signatures of Nostr events and thus to prove control of the identity (via the `npub`). Losing the nsec means losing control of that identity. The nsec must never be shared or entered into an untrusted web client; to reduce exposure, NIP-07 standardizes `window.nostr`, through which an extension can sign events without disclosing the key to the application.

entries.title: NSEQUENCE
entries.body: The `nSequence` field in a Bitcoin transaction input is used to indicate how that input is locked in time. Originally, it was intended to allow the dynamic replacement of transactions in mempools in order to enable an overlay payment system similar to Lightning. However, its use evolved with the introduction of the relative timelock via BIP-0068. The `nSequence` field can now specify a relative delay before a transaction is included in a block. This delay can be defined in terms of a number of blocks, or as a multiple of 512 seconds (that is, real time). Note that this new interpretation of the `nSequence` field is only valid if the `nVersion` field is greater than or equal to `2`. This interpretation of the `nSequence` field is done at the level of Bitcoin's consensus rules. Moreover, at the level of standardness rules, this field is also used for RBF signaling. If a transaction includes a `nSequence` lower than `0xfffffffe`, then it can be replaced via RBF on nodes that follow this policy.

entries.title: NULL DATA
entries.body: Type of Bitcoin transaction that allows a small amount of arbitrary data to be inserted using a `OP_RETURN`. Any bitcoins associated with this type of output are provably unspendable, because the `OP_RETURN` signals an invalid script.

entries.title: NULLDUMMY
entries.body: Consensus rule introduced with BIP-0147 in the SegWit soft fork that requires the dummy element ("*dummy element*") used in the `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` opcodes to be an empty byte array (`OP_0`). This measure was put in place to eliminate a malleability vector by prohibiting any value other than `OP_0` for this element.

entries.title: NUNCHUK
entries.body: Bitcoin wallet software specialized in multisig, available on desktop and mobile (iOS, Android). Nunchuk makes it easier to create and manage multisignature wallets by offering an accessible interface, even for non-technical users. The application supports most *hardware wallets* on the market and uses PSBTs to coordinate signatures between multiple devices. Nunchuk also offers collaborative features that allow several people to cosign transactions asynchronously. The software includes assisted recovery and inheritance options. It exists in a free version with the basic features and in a paid version with additional services such as assisted multisig.

entries.title: NVERSION
entries.body: The `nVersion` field in a Bitcoin transaction is used to indicate the version of the transaction format being used. It allows the network to distinguish the different evolutions of the transaction format over time, and to apply the corresponding rules. This field has an impact at the level of consensus rules: when `nVersion >= 2`, the interpretation of the `nSequence` field as a relative timelock is activated, in accordance with BIP-0068. However, no value assigned to this field causes the transaction to be invalidated. On the other hand, the `nVersion` field has standardness rules that currently accept only the values `1`, `2` and `3`. Version `3` was introduced with Bitcoin Core 28.0 for TRUC (*Topologically Restricted Until Confirmation*) transactions, as defined in BIP-0431. For the moment, this field is mainly useful for activating the `nSequence` field and for signaling TRUC transactions.

entries.title: NWC - NOSTR WALLET CONNECT
entries.body: Protocol defined by NIP-47 that allows a Lightning wallet to be controlled remotely using Nostr as the communication layer. NWC establishes an encrypted connection between a Nostr client and a Lightning wallet via Nostr relays, allowing the client to initiate payments, generate invoices and check the balance without the wallet being integrated directly into the application. The connection is authenticated by a dedicated Nostr key pair, and the messages exchanged between the client and the wallet are end-to-end encrypted. NWC is particularly useful for separating the user interface from the management of funds: a user can, for example, connect their personal Lightning node to any compatible Nostr client, which makes it easier to send zaps or make Lightning payments on the go, without exposing their private keys to the application.

entries.title: NYA - NEW YORK AGREEMENT
entries.body:
Private meeting held in 2017, bringing together more than 50 companies from the Bitcoin ecosystem, following the Consensus 2017 conference. The goal of this meeting was to end the long-standing debate on Bitcoin scaling by reaching an agreement. From this meeting came the SegWit2x proposal, drawing on the earlier SegWit2Mb proposal. It provided for two major changes to the Bitcoin protocol: 
* The adoption of SegWit with an activation threshold set at 80 percent of signaling;
* A hard fork intended to increase the maximum block size from 1 MB to 2 MB.

Despite positive signaling from more than 80% of miners, the project failed to rally sufficient consensus, leading to its abandonment. This event was interpreted by many users and developers as an attempt to attack Bitcoin.

entries.title: PRUNED NODE
entries.body:
A full node that performs pruning of the blockchain. This consists of progressively deleting the oldest blocks, after having duly verified them, in order to keep only the most recent blocks. The retention limit is set in the `bitcoin.conf` file via the `prune=n` parameter, where `n` is the maximum size taken up by the blocks in megabytes (MB). If `0` is written after this parameter, then pruning is disabled, and the node keeps the blockchain in its entirety.

Pruned nodes are sometimes considered as types of nodes different from full nodes. Using a pruned node can be particularly useful for users facing constraints in terms of storage capacity. Currently, a full node must have more than 800 GB just for storing the blockchain. A pruned node can limit the required storage to as little as 550 MB. Although it uses less disk space, a pruned node maintains a level of verification and validation similar to that of a full node. Pruned nodes therefore offer more trust to their users compared with lightweight nodes (SPV).

entries.title: ROUTING NODE
entries.body:
A Lightning Network node that forwards payments between other nodes by acting as an intermediary in the routing of transactions. When a payment is sent between two users who do not share a direct channel, the Lightning network identifies a path made up of one or more routing nodes to relay the funds step by step via HTLCs. Each routing node temporarily locks funds in a channel, then passes them on to the next node, possibly collecting small routing fees in return for this service. Routing nodes play an essential role in the connectivity of the Lightning network, because they make it possible to reach any recipient without needing a direct channel with each counterparty. A good routing node maintains sufficient liquidity and good connectivity with the other nodes of the network.

By extension, operating a routing node can be a strategy for a node operator wishing to generate income from routing fees.

entries.title: SPV NODE - LIGHTWEIGHT NODE
entries.body:
An SPV node (*Simplified Payment Verification*), sometimes called a "lightweight node", is a lightweight client of a Bitcoin node that allows users to validate transactions without having to store the entire blockchain. Instead, an SPV node stores only the block headers, and obtains information about specific transactions by querying full nodes when necessary. This verification principle is made possible by the structure of transactions in Bitcoin blocks, which are organized within a cryptographic accumulator (Merkle Tree).

This approach is advantageous for devices with limited resources, such as mobile phones. However, SPV nodes trust full nodes for the availability of information, which implies an additional level of trust and, consequently, lower security compared with full nodes. SPV nodes cannot validate transactions independently, but they can verify whether a transaction is included in a block by consulting Merkle proofs.
